title: Title, occasion and history
short: A meditation on the Fulton Ferry between Brooklyn and Manhattan, first printed in 1856 as "Sun-Down Poem" and retitled in 1860.
body: Before the Brooklyn Bridge opened (1883), commuters crossed the East River by ferry; the Fulton Ferry ran from the foot of Fulton Street in Brooklyn to Fulton Street in Manhattan. Whitman, who lived in Brooklyn and edited the Brooklyn Eagle in the 1840s, rode it constantly and later recalled his fondness for the ferries in Specimen Days. The poem first appeared in the second edition of Leaves of Grass (1856) as 'Sun-Down Poem', was renamed 'Crossing Brooklyn Ferry' in 1860, and was revised in later editions until the final text of 1881, the nine-section form printed here. Critics generally rank it among Whitman's greatest shorter poems, alongside 'Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking' and 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd'.

anchor: I see you face to face
title: face to face
short: The opening apostrophe to tide and clouds borrows Paul's phrase for full, unmediated knowledge: 'then face to face'.
body: In 1 Corinthians 13:12 Paul contrasts present knowledge, 'through a glass, darkly', with future vision 'face to face'. Whitman claims that vision now, in the ordinary world: he sees the flood-tide and the sunset clouds 'face to face'. The phrase sets the poem's central wager: that direct, bodily perception of things can join people across time. The poem ends by calling objects 'dumb, beautiful ministers', a religious image that answers the biblical echo here.

title: flood-tide and ebb-tide
short: The incoming tide; the East River is a tidal strait, and the alternation of flood and ebb shapes the poem's sense of flow and return.
body: The flood-tide is the rising tide that flows in from the sea; the ebb-tide drains back out. The East River is not a river but a tidal strait, so its current reverses with the tide. Whitman makes this daily rhythm an emblem of continuity: others 'will watch the run of the flood-tide' and the 'falling-back to the sea of the ebb-tide'. In section 9 he commands it: 'flow with the flood-tide, and ebb with the ebb-tide!' Coffman notes how the closing section repeats the earlier catalogue as imperatives, turning observation into blessing.

title: The address to future readers
short: The poem speaks directly to people who will cross the river after the poet is dead, the boldest of Whitman's addresses to the reader.
body: From the first section Whitman addresses 'you that shall cross ... years hence', and later 'you who peruse me'. The reader is imagined as a future commuter, then as a reader of this very page. The poem's tenses shift: Whitman moves from the present to the past ('I too ... cross'd the river of old') as if he were already dead, speaking back to us from our future, a shift Gilbert examines. The effect is to collapse the time between writer and reader, a theme Whitman returns to in 'Full of Life Now' and 'So Long!'.

title: the scheme
short: Each individual is "disintegrated", dissolved into separate parts, yet still part of a coherent cosmic design.
body: Section 2 opens with a paradox: the 'scheme' (plan, design) of existence is simple and well-joined, yet every self in it is 'disintegrated', that is, not whole in itself but distributed through everything. The 'impalpable sustenance' Whitman draws 'from all things' is a spiritual nourishment that cannot be touched. The idea resembles Emerson's view that each person shares in a universal 'Over-Soul', but Whitman grounds it in the senses: 'the walk in the street and the passage over the river'.

title: similitudes
short: 'Similitudes' are likenesses: the past and future resemble the present, which is why the poet can speak across time.
body: 'Similitude' (Latin similitudo, likeness) means resemblance, or an image that shows a likeness. Whitman's argument depends on sameness of experience: the tide, the gulls, the light and the crowds will be much the same for later generations, so their experience will repeat his. Section 3's repeated 'Just as you ... so I' builds this likeness into the syntax. Coffman shows how the catalogues of sections 3 and 9 mirror one another to embody it.

anchor: It avails not, time nor place
title: It avails not
short: 'Avails not' means 'is of no effect': neither time nor distance can separate the poet from his readers.
body: 'Avail' means to be of use or force. Whitman repeats the phrase in sections 3 and 5 ('distance avails not, and place avails not') as a kind of refrain, denying that the 'scores or hundreds of years between us' matter. Critics differ on how far the claim is earned: Gargano describes the poem as moving through a crisis (the 'dark patches' of section 6) to a sense of the 'everlasting moment'; Gilbert reads the poem's shifts of grammar as moving from anxiety to a sense of power over time.

title: Twelfth-month
short: December, in the Quaker way of naming months by number; the gulls are winter birds, while the ferry crossings span the seasons.
body: Quakers avoided month-names derived from pagan gods and called the months by number, so December is 'Twelfth-month'. Whitman's family admired the Quaker preacher Elias Hicks, and he heard Hicks speak as a boy, an experience he wrote about in November Boughs; he uses similar forms elsewhere ('the Ninth-month midnight' in 'Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking'). The gulls 'floating with motionless wings, oscillating their bodies' are observed with naturalist precision; the 'gradual edging toward the south' suggests winter movement. The poem mixes seasons (winter gulls, 'summer sky'), compiling many crossings into one.

title: spokes of light round the shape of my head
short: Looking down at the water, the poet sees rays of light radiating from the shadow of his own head: a natural halo.
body: When one looks at one's shadow on sunlit, rippling water, bright rays seem to stream outward from the head of the shadow (an optical effect sometimes called heiligenschein or 'holy light'). 'Centrifugal' means moving outward from a centre. The image is a democratic halo: in section 9 Whitman tells the spokes of light to diverge 'from the shape of my head, or any one's head', so that every passenger is haloed. Critics read it as a figure for the poem's sanctification of ordinary people.

title: lighter
short: A lighter is a flat-bottomed barge used to load and unload ships in harbour; 'belated', it is still working as night falls.
body: A lighter (from Dutch lichter, from lichten, to unload, lighten) is a barge for transferring cargo between ships and wharves. The catalogue of section 3 is a precise picture of the busy port of New York in the 1850s: schooners and sloops, steamers with their 'pilothouses', the steam-tug 'closely flank'd on each side by the barges', the hay-boat, the 'granite storehouses by the docks', and the foundry fires of the industrial shore. Coffman shows how the same items return in section 8 and as commands in section 9.

title: flags of all nations, lowered at sunset
short: Ships of many countries filled the harbour; by maritime custom their colours were lowered at sunset.
body: New York was the nation's greatest port, and ships 'of all nations' lay at anchor. Naval and merchant custom was to strike (lower) the ensign at sunset, which Whitman records as 'the falling of them at sunset' and later commands: 'be duly lower'd at sunset!' The internationalism of the image fits the poem's widening embrace, from the river crowd to future generations and, implicitly, to all peoples.

title: struck from the float ... held in solution
short: A chemical metaphor: individual identity is precipitated out of the universal fluid in which all being is dissolved.
body: In chemistry a substance 'held in solution' is dissolved in a liquid; it can be 'struck' or precipitated out as a solid. Whitman imagines a cosmic 'float' (a floating mass, a fluid) from which each person is struck to receive 'identity by my body'. The image explains how the self is both separate and part of the whole (compare the 'scheme' of section 2). In section 9 he calls on it: 'Suspend here and everywhere, eternal float of solution!' Critics have read the passage as Whitman's version of the soul's pre-existence, physicalised; others stress its materialism, since identity comes only 'of my body'.

title: curious abrupt questionings
short: The poet shares the reader's sudden metaphysical doubts, which come upon him in crowds or alone at night.
body: 'Curious' in Whitman often means both 'inquisitive' and 'strange'. The 'abrupt questionings' are unanswerable thoughts about identity and death. By confessing them ('I too felt'), Whitman makes his inner life another shared experience. In section 9 he addresses his own mind: 'Throb, baffled and curious brain! throw out questions and answers!', turning anxiety into energy. Gilbert's reading follows this shift from anxiety to power in the poem's grammar.

title: the dark patches
short: Section 6 is a confession of sin and doubt: the poet too has been "evil", sharing the faults the reader knows in himself.
body: The 'dark patches' are moments of depression and moral failure. Whitman lists his vices with deliberate frankness ('Blabb'd, blush'd, resented, lied, stole, grudg'd'), and admits that 'The wolf, the snake, the hog' were 'not wanting' in him. The point is not repentance but fellowship: shared weakness binds as surely as shared joy. Gargano sees this section as the poem's crisis; some critics also read the lines about young men who call him by his 'nighest name' and lean against him, and the many he loved but 'never told', as discreet references to Whitman's homosexual desire, anticipating the 'Calamus' poems of 1860.

title: knot of contrariety
short: 'Contrariety' is opposition or self-contradiction; the 'old knot' is the tangle of conflicting impulses common to all people.
body: 'Contrariety' (Latin contrarietas) means the state of being contrary: opposition, inconsistency, perverseness. To 'knit the old knot' is to tie oneself again in the familiar tangle of contradiction, a homely image (knitting) for moral confusion. Whitman's acceptance of his own contradictions recalls 'Song of Myself' ('Do I contradict myself? / Very well then I contradict myself'). The confession of section 6 is thus not a lapse in the poem's optimism but part of its argument: shared imperfection joins people as much as shared joy.

title: nighest name
short: 'Nighest' is the archaic superlative of 'nigh', near: the name closest to him, his first name, called out by friends.
body: 'Nigh' means near; 'nighest name' is the most intimate name, the given name (Walt) used by friends rather than a formal surname. Whitman, who was known as 'Walt', is recalled as being greeted familiarly by working men, ferry hands and omnibus drivers. The phrase recurs in sections 6, 8 and 9, becoming a refrain of intimacy. In section 8 he even sets these familiar voices above the gods: 'What gods can exceed these that clasp me by the hand'.

anchor: still looks back on the actor
title: the part that looks back on the actor
short: Life as a role in a play: the role one plays both shapes and reflects back on the self who plays it.
body: The old idea of the world as a stage (theatrum mundi; 'All the world's a stage', As You Like It 2.7) is turned in an unusual direction: the 'part' 'looks back on the actor or actress', as if the role observes and judges its player, or as if what we perform becomes what we are. 'The role that is what we make it, as great as we like, / Or as small' stresses freedom: the significance of a life depends on how it is played. The line returns in section 9 as a command.

sources.cite: Shakespeare, As You Like It 2.7.139-66

title: Closer yet I approach you
short: Section 7 reverses time: the poet claims he thought about the reader "before you were born", and may be looking at us now.
body: Whitman 'laid in my stores in advance', like a provident traveller, by imagining his readers before their birth. 'Who knows but I am enjoying this?' playfully suggests that the dead poet may be present at the reading. This is the climax of the poem's intimacy and has been read both as a confident prophecy of poetic immortality and as a wistful, half-joking hope. The address recalls the close of 'Song of Myself', where he tells the reader to look for him 'under your boot-soles'.

title: Manhattan / Mannahatta
short: 'Mast-hemm'd Manhattan' is ringed by ships' masts; in section 9 Whitman uses the older native form 'Mannahatta'.
body: 'Mast-hemm'd' pictures the island bordered on all sides by the masts of ships at its wharves. Whitman preferred the Lenape-derived form 'Mannahatta' (the name recorded in early Dutch sources), which he praised in a poem of that title (1860) as a word 'liquid, sane, unruly, musical'; he saw in it an authentic American name. The pairing of 'tall masts of Mannahatta' and 'beautiful hills of Brooklyn' sets the two shores the ferry joins.

sources.cite: Walt Whitman, "Mannahatta", Leaves of Grass (1860; 1881)

anchor: What the study could not teach
title: What the study could not teach
short: Whitman claims his poem achieves what scholarship and sermons cannot: a felt communion between strangers across time.
body: 'The study' is book learning, 'the preaching' organised religion. Whitman's rhetorical question ('is accomplish'd, is it not?') claims that the poem itself has made the connection that education and the pulpit only describe. The confidence, and the coy reference to what he 'promis'd without mentioning it', are typical of his conception of the poem as an act that changes the reader rather than a statement of doctrine. Compare 'Song of Myself' sect. 2: 'You shall no longer take things at second or third hand'.

sources.cite: Roger Gilbert, "From Anxiety to Power: Grammar and Crisis in 'Crossing Brooklyn Ferry'", Nineteenth-Century Literature 42 (1987)
Jerome Loving, Walt Whitman: The Song of Himself (University of California Press, 1999)
Walt Whitman, "Song of Myself", sect. 2

title: Section 9: the catalogue of imperatives
short: The images of sections 1-8 return as commands, blessing the river, gulls, ships and fires so that they continue for others.
body: The final section repeats the earlier catalogue almost item by item (tide, waves, clouds, crowds, masts, hills, gulls, summer sky in the water, spokes of light, schooners, flags, foundry fires), now in the imperative: 'Flow on', 'Frolic on', 'Burn high'. Coffman shows that this repetition, with its new confident tone, is the poem's main structural device. The commands are not orders but a blessing on the world's continuance, and they enact the poem's claim that what the poet saw will be seen again. The long lines and anaphora are typical of Whitman's free verse, often compared with the parallelism of the English Bible.

title: you who peruse me
short: The future commuter becomes the reader of the book: Whitman identifies himself with his poem.
body: 'Peruse' means to read carefully. By writing 'peruse me' rather than 'peruse this', Whitman makes the book his body, as in 'So Long!' ('Camerado, this is no book, / Who touches this touches a man'). He asks the reader to consider 'whether I may not in unknown ways be looking upon you', the most direct of his claims to be present across time. Gilbert reads the poem's shifts of address and tense as the means by which this presence is made convincing.

title: necessary film
short: The material world, or the body, is a thin covering ('film') that wraps the soul; Whitman calls it necessary rather than a barrier.
body: In much Platonic and Christian thought the body and the visible world are veils hiding spiritual reality. Whitman accepts the veil: 'Appearances ... indicate what you are', and the 'film' must 'continue to envelop the soul'. The body is 'hung' with 'our divinest aromas'. Critics read this as Whitman's transcendentalism with a materialist turn: like Emerson, he holds that natural facts are signs of spiritual facts, but unlike Emerson he insists on the value of the sign itself.

sources.cite: R. W. Emerson, Nature (1836), ch. 4 "Language"

title: dumb, beautiful ministers
short: The objects of the world are silent servants or priests that mediate between people and the soul; the poet now receives them "with free sense".
body: 'Ministers' carries both senses: servants and clergy. Things are 'dumb' because they cannot speak, yet they serve the soul and 'furnish your parts toward eternity'. The closing lines move from 'I' to 'We', a communal voice of humanity that will 'plant you permanently within us'. The poem thus ends where Emerson's Nature begins, with the world as a sacred text, but Whitman's emphasis is on love ('We fathom you not--we love you'). Critics often see this as the poem's resolution: the barrier of time is overcome by shared perception of things.
